extracted.intended_audience: students, researchers, policymakers, agency staff, and members of the public interested in federal administrative rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Explanation of the federal formal rulemaking process under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), including when formal rulemaking is required and the procedural steps agencies must follow (publication, OMB review, hearing, record, final rule).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory trigger for formal rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal rulemaking occurs 'when rules are required by statute to be made on the record after opportunity for an agency hearing.' (APA; U.S. Code § 556 and § 557).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the enabling statute requires rules to be made on the record after a hearing; if so, formal rulemaking must be used (examples include certain ratemaking rules and food additive regulations). If the statute does not require an on-the-record hearing, agencies generally follow informal rulemaking unless hybrid procedures are specified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hearing in lieu of comment period (trial-like proceedings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal rulemaking requires consideration of a proposed agency action during a trial-like hearing process, which occurs in place of the informal rulemaking comment period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The hearing is presided over by an agency official or an administrative law judge (ALJ) and includes opportunities for participants to state positions, present evidence, and undergo cross-examination. The proceeding is similar to a court trial: oaths, subpoenas, cross-examination, and an evidentiary record are expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presiding officer / ALJ authority and evidentiary control
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency official or an administrative law judge presides over the hearing and 'traditionally has the authority to administer oaths, issue subpoenas, and exclude "irrelevant, immaterial, or unduly repetitious evidence."'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presiding officers control admissibility of evidence and may exclude evidence that is irrelevant, immaterial, or repetitious. They use subpoenas, administer oaths, and manage cross-examination to ensure a reliable record for decisionmaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on ex parte communications during the hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal rulemaking prohibits any communication between affected parties and agency officials, known as ex parte communications, during the hearing process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure no off-the-record or unilateral communications occur between interested parties and decisionmaking agency officials during the formal hearing; communications must be made through the record in the proceeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record and transcript requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A transcript of the hearing must record evidence and testimony in order to serve as the basis for the presiding officer's decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create and preserve a full transcript and evidentiary record (written exhibits, sworn testimony, cross-examination) so that fact findings and conclusions in the final rule are supported by the on-the-record proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation and publication of proposed rule and notice of formal proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: If the suggested agency action requires formal rulemaking, the agency must prepare a proposed rule outlining the recommended action and prepare to publish a notice of upcoming formal rulemaking proceedings including information about the proposed rule, the time and place of the hearing, and the agency's legal authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposed rule and the notice must be published in the Federal Register; they may be published as a single document or as separate documents. The notice must give clear procedural details (what is proposed, when/where the hearing will occur, and the statutory authority).

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal Register publication requirements and standard format
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed and final rules follow a standard format that begins with a preamble (which includes several subsections), continues with a statement of authority, and concludes with the full text or narrative description of the measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft preambles with appropriate subsections (e.g., background, statutory authority, summary of comments/hearing record), include a statement of authority, and provide the full regulatory text or a narrative description per Federal Register conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content required in final rule (rationale and findings from the record)
rubrics_metrics.description: In formal rulemaking, the final rule must include information about the rationale for the regulation as well as relevant fact findings and conclusions from the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final rule must tie conclusions and regulatory choices to the evidentiary record created at hearing; include explicit findings of fact and legal rationale demonstrating how the record supports the agency's determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: OMB review for significant rules (proposed and final)
rubrics_metrics.description: Executive Order 12866 requires that the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) review any proposed rules (and final rules) that are deemed to be significant rules. The OMB has 90 days (with a possible 30 day extension) to complete its review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proposed rule cannot be published in the Federal Register until OMB completes its review without recommendations or the review period expires. OMB may return a proposed or draft final rule to the agency for reconsideration if the analysis is faulty or not aligned with presidential priorities; agencies must reconsider rules returned with comments or changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: OMB review exceptions (independent agencies)
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB review under Executive Order 12866 applies except to independent federal agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the issuing agency is an independent agency; if so, the OMB review requirement for significant rules does not apply, though other review or coordination obligations may exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission to Congress and GAO before effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: In most cases, a final rule cannot take effect until the rule has been submitted to both houses of Congress and the General Accounting Office (GAO). After publication in the Federal Register, a final rule is added to the Code of Federal Regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for any statutory or procedural waiting periods and transmittal obligations (Congress/GAO review) before the effective date; ensure proper transmittal and Federal Register publication to codify the rule in the CFR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nine-step rulemaking procedure (relationship to informal rulemaking)
rubrics_metrics.description: The formal rulemaking process mirrors the informal rulemaking process, which OIRA breaks down into nine steps; the difference is step six, which calls for a hearing during formal rulemaking and a comment period during informal rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the standard sequence: (1) idea for a rule, (2) discussion, (3) preparation of proposed rule and notice of formal proceedings, (4) OMB review of proposed rule (if applicable), (5) publication of proposed rule and notice, (6) hearing, (7) preparation of final rule, (8) OMB review of final rule (if applicable), (9) publication of final rule. Treat the hearing as the central distinguishing procedural element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of rulemaking initiation
rubrics_metrics.description: A federal agency's initial motivation to create, modify, or repeal a rule may come from several sources: Congress, an agency's internal priorities, external factors (new technology, scientific data, accidents), required reviews, lawsuits, petitions, OIRA prompt letters, or recommendations from other agencies/committees/groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and document the initiating source(s) in the proposed rule preamble and administrative record to establish the administrative context and need for the rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication triggers under APA §552 (what must appear in Federal Register)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provisions of the APA in U.S. Code §552 require publication in the Federal Register of: 'Substantive rules of general applicability; Interpretive rules; Statements of general policy; Rules of procedure; Information about forms; Information concerning agency organization and methods of operation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the agency action fits one of these categories; if so, prepare Federal Register publication materials accordingly and include required informational elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of hybrid procedures when specified
rubrics_metrics.description: Hybrid rulemaking blends specified elements of formal rulemaking into the informal rulemaking process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where statutes or agency practice permit, use hybrid procedures to incorporate certain formal elements (e.g., limited hearings or additional evidentiary steps) into otherwise informal rulemakings; document the legal basis for any hybrid approach.
